1.t: Unit 1: Role-playing a teen's choice about sharing personal details
1.y: In the role of a teen, students choose from three options and say why. Partial at this level, as the options are given.

2.t: Unit 4: Designing a business around a social issue they choose
2.y: Groups pick a social issue and apply what they learnt to design a business that passes on its profit. On paper only, so partial at this level.

1.t: Unit 1: Role-playing two neighbours at odds over their rights
1.y: Students act as an online poster and her neighbour before discussing how to respect a neighbour's rights and settle the problem.

2.t: Unit 3: Comparing the titles given to notable people
2.y: Students discuss how titles for people who serve others are alike and differ. A comparison of ideas, so a partial fit at this level.

2.t: Unit 3: Figures who contributed to Singapore's progress
2.y: Students learn about historical figures through a video and a game, then discuss their contributions to Singapore. One-sided, so partial at this level.

3.t: Unit 6: Can Singapore live without depending on other countries?
3.y: Students discuss whether we can live without other countries and how far Singapore depends on them. Discussion, with views limited to this question.

1.t: Unit 1: Discussing the law on maintaining elderly parents
1.y: Students read about the Singapore Maintenance of Parents Act and discuss whether parents may expect support, if suing children is fair and other ways out. Discussion only.

1.t: Unit 2: Debating if technology suits youth involvement in Malay arts
1.y: Students discuss whether technology is suitable to draw youth into Malay arts and heritage, using news articles. Discussion only; no more than one view is required.

2.t: Unit 4: Groups agree on an issue and a business plan together
2.y: Groups choose one social issue, give reasons and build one plan to present. Handling disagreement is not spelled out.

1.t: Unit 2: Planning a self-expression piece as a group
1.y: Groups choose how to express themselves, why, the theme and each member's role, then make the piece. The guide allows individual work too.

3.t: WA3 authentic task: team debate on a given motion, with prepared scripts
3.y: Teams argue a stated side of a motion in set speaking roles, with key terms defined, main ideas for both sides listed, and rebuttal or interjection in response to opponents. Scored on team strategy too.

2.t: WA2: Functional writing, an email to a stated reader
2.y: Students write an email to a stated reader, covering the required points for a clear purpose. One way only: a single written message.

2.t: Oral: conversation on a video, giving experience, ideas and an opinion
2.y: In a conversation with the examiner, students share a personal experience, then explain or suggest, then say whether they agree with a statement and why.

2.t: Unit 3: Presenting an infographic on a role model to emulate
2.y: In pairs or groups students choose a person to follow and make an infographic with a thinking routine, then present it. Audience is the class.

2.t: Unit 4: Presenting a community business plan and giving peer feedback
2.y: Groups choose a format (slides, poster, audio, advert, post, infographic) to present their plan, and classmates give views using a presentation rubric.

4.t: EOY Paper 1 Section A: Functional email or reply, choice of two
4.y: Students choose one of two situations and write an email or reply to a stated reader for a clear purpose, covering the points required. One way only: a single written message.

1.t: Unit 2: Fitting group roles to members' strengths
1.y: The planning model assigns roles by what each member does well (one writes, one plays, one acts). Only partly CCI 4: the guide models it and students may work alone.

2.t: Unit 4: Planning a business that helps the community
2.y: In groups students pick a social issue, give reasons, design a business and explain how profit is made and passed on, then present. Plan only; nothing is run.

1.t: Unit 1: Searching news on the law about supporting parents
1.y: Students search news pages for articles on the Maintenance of Parents Act and share what they find; the guide marks this as an inquiry experience.

1.t: Unit 2: Searching news on youth, technology and Malay heritage
1.y: Students search news pages for articles on youth and technology in Malay heritage and arts, share in pairs and comment on peers' replies; marked as an inquiry experience.

2.t: Unit 4: Investigating a social issue and designing a helping business
2.y: The guide ties this to inquiry: students investigate and explore to help people in difficulty, then plan a business around an issue.

3.t: Unit 5: Searching for the logical cause of a mystery sound
3.y: Students give popular and logical explanations for marble-like night sounds in flats, then search the Internet for the reason and discuss it with a partner.

3.t: Unit 6: Researching at home where everyday products come from
3.y: Students do a flipped home study on where household products come from and share findings, then groups search news for creative answers to food shortage.

2.t: Unit 4: Watching a video on community businesses and asking a question
2.y: After a video on businesses that help the community, each student names one interesting point and asks one question, which the unit then follows up.

3.t: Unit 5: Discussing the causes of famous mysteries
3.y: Students see mysteries such as the Bermuda Triangle and discuss what might have caused them, then look for logical explanations through the unit.

2.t: Unit 4: Presenting plans, peer feedback and reflecting
2.y: Groups present their business plan, classmates comment, and students reflect on what they used to think and what they improve.

1.t: Unit 2: Making their own self-expression piece
1.y: Students choose the form (performance, recording, drawing, poem) and theme, make a piece and write a short description of it.

1.t: Unit 2: Telling peers what they appreciate in their work
1.y: Students share their pieces and reply to classmates with one thing they appreciate and a word of motivation.

2.t: Unit 4: Designing a business to serve people in need
2.y: Students plan a business that serves a group in difficulty and think about the values needed to serve the community.

3.t: Unit 6: Writing to an organisation to join and support its event
3.y: Students draft a formal email to an organisation they choose, stating why they want to join and what they could do to support its event. One-way writing.

1.t: Unit 1: Explaining why three groups differ on AI for schoolwork
1.y: Students read three groups' views on whether AI tools encourage cheating and explain why the views differ, using a perspective-taking organiser.

1.t: Unit 2: Applying land-use ideas to plan a small room at home
1.y: After learning how Singapore uses limited space, pairs or groups pick a scenario and draw a plan making the most of a room, then gather feedback.

1.t: Unit 1: Testing an event plan against a sudden Wi-Fi failure
1.y: Groups present their plan, then test it against losing Internet or Wi-Fi and think of an extra plan to keep the attendance task going.

1.t: Unit 2: Groups decide on a room and a plan for it together
1.y: Groups settle which room to use, what space to exploit and why, then prepare one prototype drawing. Partial: disagreement is not addressed.

1.t: Unit 2: Why each person's role matters to Singapore's survival
1.y: Students explain how individuals can play a part as citizens in Singapore's survival and exchange reasoned views. Partial at this level.

1.t: Unit 2: Reacting to how Singapore uses limited land
1.y: Students read how Singapore uses limited land (reclamation, tall buildings, underground caverns), react with reasons and suggest other ways. Mostly own view, little on other perspectives.

1.t: Unit 2: Sorting Total Defence pillars and what citizens do in each
1.y: Students explore Total Defence and the part each citizen plays, such as national service or volunteering. Roles only: nothing is organised.

1.t: Oral: conversation on a video, giving experience, ideas and an opinion
1.y: In a conversation with the examiner, students share a personal experience, then explain or suggest, then say whether they agree with a statement and why.

1.t: Unit 1: Presenting problem solutions with and without technology
1.y: Groups solve sudden event problems with and without technology, compare both ways and present, then reflect after each presentation. Partly one-way.

2.t: TP Paper 1: Functional email, choice of two
2.y: Students choose one of two situations and write an email or reply to a stated reader for a clear purpose, covering the points required. One way only: a single written message.

1.t: Unit 3: Comparing Malay life in Singapore and abroad
1.y: After a video call among teens from different countries, students compare Malay values, language and culture in Singapore and elsewhere and say what they would present.

1.t: Unit 1: Asking why old gadget images count as fiction
1.y: Pairs study images of old gadgets, say why they are called fiction, then compare with a page of everyday reality; the guide marks this as an inquiry experience.

1.t: Unit 3: Deciding if teens with DNA profiles count as Malay
1.y: Students study four teens' DNA profiles, find evidence and argue whether each can be called Malay, which opens the unit's identity questions.

1.t: Unit 2: Searching for creative ways to use small spaces
1.y: Students search the Internet for creative ways Singapore or other countries use small spaces and note them for the next group design task.

1.t: Unit 2: Reflecting on themselves as role models and citizens
1.y: Students reflect on being a role model for others and on their own part in Singapore's future, linking what they can do to making a difference.

1.t: Unit 3: Naming their own part in keeping Malay identity alive
1.y: Students say what part they can play in keeping their community's identity going, wherever they might live.

1.t: Unit 2: Designing their own room plan in a tool of their choice
1.y: Students choose a room and scenario, then make a prototype plan by hand or with a free digital tool. A product they own.

1.t: Tamil and me: How written and spoken Tamil differ
1.y: Students discuss how words change between written and spoken Tamil, then rework a dialogue for speech.

3.t: Water management: Comparing ancient Tamil and Singapore water plans
3.y: Students compare water management plans of the ancient Tamils with Singapore’s water-saving plans, and say what the ancient plans teach us.

2.t: Goals: Deciding what to do in everyday situations
2.y: Students work through situations such as a schoolmate short of money for food, and think through how to solve the problem. The guide tags responsible decision-making.

1.t: New beginnings: Recording views on a CCA
1.y: Students record their views in spoken Tamil, using words that suit the situation.

1.t: Harvest festival: Designing and presenting a brochure
1.y: Students design and present a brochure for a given situation.

1.t: Tamil and me: Exchanging views orally
1.y: Students exchange views orally in response to set questions.

2.t: Goals: Email to a friend on thoughts and feelings
2.y: Students express thoughts and feelings in a fitting style.

2.t: Oral exam: Giving and justifying views on sport and health
2.y: After a video on sports, students say which they would like to play and why, then say whether they agree that sport benefits body and mind.

3.t: Oral presentation: The CCA I like, recorded with slides
3.y: Students build slides with examples, then record their presentation.

3.t: The Internet: Making a poster on Internet use
3.y: Students gather information and make a poster on Internet use.

3.t: Water management: Writing an event article
3.y: Students write an article that suits a given situation.

4.t: End-of-year email: Reply to a friend
4.y: Students reply to a friend for a set purpose, sharing useful holiday activities or advising on healthy living. They choose 1 of 2.

4.t: End-of-year essay: An incident and the lesson learnt
4.y: Students write at least 180 words, such as on an unexpected incident and the lesson learnt.

4.t: End-of-year comprehension: Explaining ideas in own words
4.y: Students read for meaning and explain in their own words, such as why thrift matters.

1.t: Harvest festival: Conversation on Pongal
1.y: Students keep a conversation going by explaining and asking questions. The guide tags cross-cultural understanding.

2.t: Goals: Expressing ideas to suit different situations
2.y: Students express ideas and feelings to suit different situations. The guide tags social awareness.

2.t: Oral exam: Encouraging a friend to take up sport
2.y: Students say how they would encourage a friend who has no interest in sport.

4.t: End-of-year email, option 2: Advising a friend on health
4.y: Students write to a close friend whose health is suffering, advising on healthy living. Not all students choose this option.

3.t: Water management: Building on other groups’ ideas at learning corners
3.y: Groups discuss a question and write their ideas at a learning corner, then move on, read what others wrote and add their own, before returning to sum up.

1.t: Harvest festival: Pongal and cultural understanding
1.y: Students watch a video on Pongal and talk about the festival. The guide tags civic literacy, global awareness and cross-cultural understanding.

1.t: Tamil and me: The role of Tamils in Singapore
1.y: Students discuss how Tamils helped Singapore progress, then watch a video on their role, Tamil as one of four official languages, and Tamil place names.

3.t: Water management: Discussing water saving
3.y: Students watch a video and discuss water saving in class. The guide tags civic literacy and global awareness.

3.t: Water management: Water rationing and water saving in Singapore
3.y: Groups discuss whether Singapore uses water rationing and why, and what Singapore does to save water.

3.t: Water management: Singapore’s reservoirs, plants and NEWater
3.y: Students discuss how Singapore meets its water needs through reservoirs, treatment plants and NEWater.

3.t: Water management: How countries manage water
3.y: Students read how different countries manage water and answer questions. The guide tags civic literacy and global awareness.

2.t: Keeping healthy: Students list what they know and want to know about food
2.y: Before the reading, students write what they already know and what they want to know about food on a KWL form, then share it.

3.t: The internet: Students present a poster built from what they gathered on internet use
3.y: Students turn the information they gathered into a poster and share it with the class, so they synthesise and present their findings.

3.t: Water management: Groups judge other groups' findings and evidence and comment
3.y: After groups submit their findings, other groups assess the ideas and evidence and give comments against a rubric. This is peer feedback on findings.

1.t: Tamil and me: Students find how written Tamil words are said at home
1.y: As an extension, students list ten written Tamil words and find out how each is spoken in their own homes. Optional, so partial.

2.t: Keeping healthy: Pairs gather extra information online to build an essay or story
2.y: Pairs collect more information on the theme "health is wealth" using computers, add it to their mind map, and use it to write a piece.

3.t: The internet: Students collect information on internet uses to make a poster
3.y: Students gather information on what the internet is used for and turn it into a poster they present to the class.

3.t: Water management: Groups research ancient Tamil and Singapore water schemes
3.y: Groups research set questions comparing ancient Tamil water management with Singapore's, gathering evidence on their own devices and recording it. Offered as an online option.

1.t: New beginnings: Groups write class slogans, get peer feedback, then improve them
1.y: Groups write slogans, present them, hear classmates' comments and questions, then revise their own work. Feedback leads to improvement.

1.t: Tamil and me: Students write a personal pledge to keep learning Tamil
1.y: Students create a pledge stating what they will do to keep learning Tamil, which is a personal commitment to continue their own learning.

2.t: Goals: Students set a goal for the year and choose life skills to reach it
2.y: Students decide on their own goal for the year, name the life skills that will help, and share it. Friends may suggest other skills.

2.t: Goals: Students write an email to support a friend facing a challenge
2.y: Students plan and write an email to a friend who is struggling, covering the challenge, who can help and what advice they would give. Practises supporting a peer.

2.t: Kings of Tamil Nadu: Groups compare a king's court with Parliament today
2.y: Groups compare who sat in a royal court with who sits in Parliament today, and their duties, then share and answer classmates' questions.

2.t: Yesterday, today, tomorrow: Groups compare traditional Tamil games with electronic games
2.y: Groups find how playing traditional games differs from electronic games and weigh the pros and cons for young people, then record their thinking.

3.t: Financial literacy: Students compare buying in a shop with buying online
3.y: From their own experience, students say how shopping in person differs from shopping online and what they weigh up. An opening discussion, so partial.

3.t: Youth and society: Groups compare two newspaper reports
3.y: Groups discuss how two newspaper reports are alike and different, then share with the class. A comparison of reports; the link to a view is not asked for.

3.t: Financial literacy: Groups decide what to buy and cut on a fixed budget
3.y: Working within a set budget, groups weigh choices, decide what to drop and how much to save, then report the challenges they met and how they solved them.

2.t: Yesterday, today, tomorrow: Groups solve a spun situation using a spun object and chance
2.y: Groups spin wheels for a situation, an object and an opportunity, then solve the situation using the other two. This is a chance-driven, unfamiliar problem.

1.t: Friendship: Pairs role-play telling a friend they are hurt, advising and praising
1.y: Pairs act out set situations: reaching agreement after a difference, telling a friend how a hurt felt, advising a friend and praising a good deed.

1.t: Protecting the environment: Groups pool and refine one speaker's views
1.y: Students pick one speaker from a dialogue and sum up their views, then join others who chose the same speaker to refine the points together and share.

2.t: Newspaper article: Group drafting and peer editing
2.y: Groups peer-edit the article together and share a single video presentation, taking in each other's suggestions to finish a common product. Evidence of disagreement handling is limited.

2.t: Yesterday, today, tomorrow: Groups decide what features their e-advertisement needs
2.y: Groups analyse a given situation, plan an e-advertisement, decide which elements it needs and build a draft. The guide does not mention handling disagreement.

3.t: Financial literacy: Groups agree what to buy with 50 coins and what to cut to save
3.y: Groups jointly choose 15 items within a budget, then decide which five to drop and how much to save, then report challenges and group experience.

1.t: Protecting the environment: Students look up what Singapore does to protect nature
1.y: Students find evidence of Singapore's green efforts, including at Changi Airport, then discuss it in groups and answer classmates' questions.

1.t: Protecting the environment: Students sum up four speakers on Singapore's environment
1.y: Students read a dialogue with four speakers on protecting Singapore's environment, choose one and sum up that person's views, then compare in groups.

3.t: Youth and society: Students discuss how young people can contribute to society
3.y: After reading a news item and posting their thoughts, students discuss how today's youth can contribute to society. A single issue, with views from classmates.

3.t: Youth and society: Students explain efforts to help Singapore's Tamil community thrive
3.y: Students discuss what is done to help the Tamil community in Singapore flourish and why, using current news as evidence. One viewpoint, so partial.

1.t: Email reply: Replying to a friend's email for set purposes
1.y: Students read a friend's email and write a reply covering each purpose set, such as sharing experience or giving advice, in a friendly register. One-way writing to a named reader.

1.t: Friendship: Groups present their ideas on friendship as a poster, skit or dialogue
1.y: Groups discuss a chosen question on friendship and present it in a form of their choice. Classmates respond and ask questions, so the audience is the class.

1.t: Friendship: Groups design a vlog script for a given situation and share it
1.y: Groups design a dialogue, story or interview for a vlog suited to a given context, share it with the class and improve it after comments.

1.t: Hobbies: Students write a news report on benefits of hobbies for readers
1.y: Students turn information gathered into a news report with the features of the form, then may post it for peers to read and comment. Largely one-way writing.

1.t: Protecting the environment: Students write an official email for a given situation
1.y: Students learn the features of an official email and write one for a stated situation. This is one-way writing for a stated purpose and recipient.

2.t: Oral exam: Answering examiner questions on a video
2.y: After a short video, students answer examiner questions: their reaction or experience, what they suggest, and whether they agree with a given view, giving reasons. Spoken, with the examiner.

2.t: Newspaper article and video: Telling a school community member's story
2.y: Students interview a real person, then convey the story in a newspaper article and a recorded presentation for readers and viewers. Largely one-way presentation to an audience.

2.t: Kings of Tamil Nadu: Pairs write a circular and present it to the class
2.y: Pairs prepare a circular for a given situation and present it. Classmates comment and ask questions, then the pair improves the circular.

2.t: Yesterday, today, tomorrow: Students rank inventions and revise after peers' views
2.y: Students rank inventions by importance with evidence, read classmates' posts, comment, then revisit and change their own view where needed.

4.t: Email: Replying to a friend or writing in a given role to a stated reader
4.y: Students choose one email task: reply to a friend, or write in an imagined role to a stated reader. One-way writing for a set purpose and reader.

3.t: Financial literacy: Students write a funding-request email, designed first in groups
3.y: Groups design a funding-request email for a stated situation, then each student writes one and shares it. Purpose and recipient are set by the task.

3.t: Youth and society: Students write a report on a school event
3.y: Students learn the purpose and steps of a report and write one on a school event from a given situation. One-way writing.

2.t: Kings of Tamil Nadu: Groups compare roles in a royal court with those in Parliament
2.y: Groups compare who sat in a king's court and who sits in Parliament today, and compare their responsibilities. A comparison of civic roles only, nothing organised.

1.t: Hobbies: Students interview parents or grandparents about their childhood pastimes
1.y: Students interview parents or grandparents about childhood pastimes, take notes on games played by family or neighbours, and discuss them in class.

1.t: Hobbies: Students gather hobby information from five classmates for a news report
1.y: Each student picks five classmates, collects what hobbies they have and the benefits gained, then uses it to write a news report.

1.t: Protecting the environment: Students look up answers to three questions on nature
1.y: Students search for answers to three set questions on nature and the environment, write them in the textbook and discuss in groups. The guide labels this lesson inquiry-based.

1.t: Protecting the environment: Students find evidence of Singapore's green efforts
1.y: Students individually search for evidence that Changi Airport is green and for Singapore's efforts to protect the environment, then discuss in groups.

2.t: Interview: Finding out a school community member's story first-hand
2.y: Students interview a real person live in Tamil, ask their own questions and make sense of the replies to build the article. They find out first-hand.

2.t: Kings of Tamil Nadu: Students look up the kings in the pictures before class
2.y: Before class, students search online for details of the kings shown in the opening pictures, then share their findings with the class.

2.t: Yesterday, today, tomorrow: Groups work out a text's main idea and compare three texts
2.y: Groups read their own text, find its main idea and the clues, then read two others and compare. The guide labels this the 5E inquiry method. Texts only.

2.t: Yesterday, today, tomorrow: Groups collect data on old and electronic games
2.y: Groups use their own devices to collect data on three questions about traditional and electronic games, including pros and cons for young people.

3.t: Financial literacy: Groups read chosen texts, explain main ideas and point to clues
3.y: Groups pick texts from nine on financial literacy, explain each main idea and point to the clues that showed it. The guide names this the 5E inquiry method.

2.t: Video and reflection: Sharing the story found and reflecting on it
2.y: Groups share what they found in a recorded presentation and write an individual reflection in class on the project.

2.t: Yesterday, today, tomorrow: Groups share findings, answer questions and are evaluated
2.y: Groups share what they found with the class, others ask questions, and classmates and teacher assess the work against a rubric. This is the 5E method.

2.t: Yesterday, today, tomorrow: Groups read and comment on other groups' entries
2.y: After groups post their views on games, other groups read them and respond with comments, and the teacher pulls the ideas together.

1.t: Protecting the environment: Groups share findings and answer classmates' questions
1.y: Groups share what they gathered on recycling and green efforts. Classmates comment and ask questions, and the group explains its findings.

3.t: Financial literacy: Groups share with the class and peers question them
3.y: Groups share their discussion with the class and others ask questions to clear doubts. Follows the 5E inquiry method named in the guide.

1.t: Friendship: Students state agree or disagree on friendship ideas before reading
1.y: Before reading, students mark whether they agree with ideas about friendship, then check the text, cite the page and explain if their stance holds. One text only, so modest.

1.t: Protecting the environment: Students answer an open question on nature's gifts
1.y: Before class, students answer on a shared board what gifts nature has given us; the lesson then builds on the answers in group work on a poem. The guide labels this inquiry-based.

1.t: Friendship: Pairs practise repairing a hurt, advising and praising a friend
1.y: Pairs act out telling a friend they felt hurt and hearing the reply, advising a friend who erred and praising a friend's good deed.

3.t: Youth and society: Students reflect on the unit and get one-to-one feedback
3.y: Students write what they make of their learning in the unit, share it, and then get individual feedback from the teacher on what to work towards.

2.t: Newspaper article: Drafting, peer editing and reflecting
2.y: Groups draft the article, peer-edit it and revise before submission, then each writes an individual reflection on the work.

2.t: Kings of Tamil Nadu: Pairs improve their circular after class comments
2.y: After classmates comment on a circular, the pair rewrites it and hands in an improved version.

1.t: Friendship: Groups improve their vlog plan after class and teacher comments
1.y: Groups design vlog content, share it, hear classmates' comments and the teacher's improvement points, then refine their work.

2.t: Newspaper article: Choosing an interviewee and making an own product
2.y: Groups choose their own interviewee from the school community and make a newspaper article and video that they own.

1.t: Friendship: Students choose how to record their own thinking about friendship
1.y: Students pick their own form for their thoughts on friendship (a word, phrase, slogan, poem or picture), then share it with the class.

3.t: Financial literacy: Students choose three of nine financial texts to read
3.y: Students choose which three of nine financial-literacy texts to read before class and join the matching group.

terms.1: The arts · Me and my relationships · Leadership qualities · WA1
terms.2: Living in harmony with nature · The Tamil way of life · WA2 · Oral
terms.3: Mental well-being · Tamil and the world · AA

1.t: Leadership qualities: Students compare ideas in a reading with what happens today
1.y: A stated lesson aim: students compare the ideas in a reading with present-day practice and comment. No change of view is required, so partial at this level.

1.t: The arts: Students compare old and modern paintings, then picture what comes next
1.y: Students state similarities and differences between old and today's paintings, then predict what follows digital art. Only partly links the comparison to a changed view.

2.t: The Tamil way of life: Students compare Tamils' service in a reading with today's news
2.y: Students bring news on the community service of Tamils today and compare the ideas in a reading with present-day practice. Partial at this level.

2.t: The Tamil way of life: Students compare ancient values with how they are followed today
2.y: Students link old values to present-day life through a viewpoints routine; the comparison is stated, but how it changes their view is not.

3.t: Mental well-being: Students compare ideas in a letter with what happens today
3.y: A stated lesson aim: students compare a letter's ideas on kind and proud minds with present-day practice and comment. No change of view is required.

1.t: Me and my relationships: Students plan a family get-together for a given situation
1.y: Students apply what they learnt to plan a family gathering that fits a set situation and justify the plan to the class. Partial at this level.

3.t: Tamil and the world: Students plan a programme for an event they choose
3.y: Students pick an event, plan its programme and write the host's speech, applying what they learnt to a new occasion. Partial at this level.

1.t: The arts: Students respond to information on the Singapore Youth Festival
1.y: Students read about the Singapore Youth Festival, answer with See-Think-Wonder and react to peers' views with reasons. Only partly about an issue for Singapore.

2.t: Living in harmony with nature: Students discuss Singapore's five-year green plan
2.y: Students discuss the steps Singapore will take on its green plan over the next five years. One account of the issue, so partial at this level.

2.t: Living in harmony with nature: Students think of other ways to raise green awareness
2.y: After reading how nature is cared for in Singapore, students think through and discuss what else could raise awareness and protect greenery.

3.t: Debate: Arguing for or against a set question on culture in Singapore
3.y: Students argue for or against a set question on culture in Singapore, with both sides heard. Partial at Level 4: the tension is aired, not worked through.

2.t: Oral exam: Answering examiner questions on a video
2.y: After a short video, students answer examiner questions: their reaction or experience, what they suggest, and whether they agree with a given view, giving reasons. Spoken, with the examiner.

3.t: Debate speech: Arguing a position with reasons and evidence
3.y: Students prepare and deliver a debate speech of about 2 to 3 minutes with reasons and evidence, and rebut the other side. Spoken to a class audience.

3.t: Mental well-being: Two teams may debate whether social media wastes students' time
3.y: Teams argue opposite sides on social media and time use. The guide offers this as an option alongside a written argument essay.

3.t: Tamil and the world: Students write and deliver a host's speech for an event
3.y: Students write and present a programme host's speech for an event they choose, following the writing tips. One-way to a class audience.

1.t: The arts: Students agree or disagree with peers' posts and give reasons
1.y: On a class board, students react to classmates' views by agreeing with reasons, disagreeing with reasons, or replying.

1.t: Me and my relationships: Teams debate after choosing a stance and refining arguments
1.y: Students choose a stance, join a team, gather and refine arguments, then debate in class with teacher feedback. Stated position and audience.

1.t: Leadership qualities: Students rank qualities and may change after hearing others
1.y: Students rank nine leadership qualities, give reasons, listen to classmates' reasons and may change their ranking, saying why.

1.t: Leadership qualities: Students write a short speech and deliver it to the class
1.y: Students study the features of a short speech, write one for a given occasion and deliver it. One-way, to a class audience.

1.t: The arts: Pairs, then fours, then the class decide why folk arts must be preserved
1.y: Pairs trade at least three views, agree or disagree with evidence, then fours reach a decision and the whole class settles on reasons together.

2.t: The Tamil way of life: Groups agree one view on how old values live on today
2.y: Group members each give a view on harmony, charity or hospitality today, discuss and must reach one agreed view before sharing with the class.

3.t: Mental well-being: Groups respond to a person's decision in a written case
3.y: Groups write three thoughts on a person's decision, two messages to say to them and a title, then answer classmates' questions. A written case, not a real person.

1.t: The arts: Students note what they know, what puzzles them and what to explore
1.y: Before class, students record what they know about paintings, what puzzles them and what they want to find out, then react to peers' posts.

1.t: Me and my relationships: Students write their own questions about relationships first
1.y: Students individually jot the questions that occur to them about relationships, then put them to a partner. The questions come from the students.

2.t: Living in harmony with nature: Students list what they know and want to know on greenery
2.y: Using a KWL chart, students write what they know and what they want to know about green Singapore from pictures and share it.

3.t: Mental well-being: Students list what they know and want to know before reading a speech
3.y: With a KWL form, students write what they know and what they want to know about mental well-being, then read to find answers.

3.t: Mental well-being: Students use KWL again before reading a letter on kind and proud minds
3.y: Students write what they know about key words from a letter, then what they want to know, and read to find answers.

1.t: Me and my relationships: Students gather points for a debate on their own devices
1.y: After picking a stance, groups collect arguments on their devices and share them on a shared board before debating.

2.t: Living in harmony with nature: Students search images and news for green Singapore facts
2.y: Students use image search to collect information on the pictures in the opening pages and record it in the chart.

2.t: Living in harmony with nature: Students record what they learned and share in groups
2.y: After the lessons, students fill in what they have learned about green Singapore and share it in groups, closing the KWL cycle.

3.t: Mental well-being: Students write what they learned and share it with the class
3.y: After reading, students write what they learned, compare it with what they wanted to know and share both with the class.

1.t: The arts: Students reflect on the unit and get one-to-one feedback
1.y: Students comment on their own performance in writing, share it, and then get individual feedback from the teacher on how to improve.

1.t: The arts: Pairs choose the maker, audience, form and topic of their own podcast series
1.y: Pairs pick who makes the podcast, the audience, format and topic, then design its logo, blurb and episode plan, an item they own. Recording it is an extension.

1.t: Leadership qualities: Students may choose a novel to read through the year
1.y: Students may pick their own novel at the start of the year and later compare it with a short story. A choice offered to teachers as an option.

3.t: Tamil and the world: Students create their own slogan praising Tamil
3.y: Students write a slogan praising Tamil in a form of their choice (phrase or verse) on a drawn tote bag and explain it to the class.

3.t: Tamil and the world: Students choose a school or community event to plan and host
3.y: Students choose an event, plan its programme, write the host's speech and present it. The choice of event is theirs.

1.t: Me and my relationships: Pairs ask each other their own questions about relationships
1.y: Each student writes questions on relationships, then partners take turns asking and answering and report what they learnt from each other.

1.t: Me and my relationships: Students talk with family for two minutes and record it
1.y: Students hold a short conversation with family members, note it down and record it, then upload both for the teacher's comments.

1.t: Me and my relationships: Students plan a family get-together and may carry it out
1.y: Students plan a family gathering for a given situation and explain their reasons; as an extension they hold it and share the family's reaction.

3.t: Mental well-being: Students try 30 mind-care activities over 30 days and report back
3.y: Students carry out thirty mental-health activities across thirty days and share their experience each week. The guide sets this as an extension.

3.t: Mental well-being: Students design a cup showing their current mood
3.y: Students design a cup showing their present state of mind, present it, and classmates respond. This is naming and sharing feelings.

1.t: Nation-building: Students judge an interviewer's conduct, then role-play both sides
1.y: Students say what an interviewer should and should not have done in a news interview, then take turns as interviewer and interviewee. Partial at this level.

1.t: Traditions and customs: Students run a discussion and reach decisions on evidence
1.y: In a student-run circle, students agree or disagree with each other using evidence and reach a decision. The guide does not set a way to handle conflict.

2.t: Entrepreneurship: Groups weigh each member's ranking and share a group stance
2.y: After ranking two qualities alone, students hear peers, may change their view and one member presents the group's stance with evidence. Consensus is implied.

1.t: Nation-building: Students link a poem to Singapore's history and discuss national growth
1.y: Students recall Singapore's history, connect it to a poem and discuss how the nation grew, using pictures. One account of the issue, so partial at this level.

1.t: Nation-building: Students read a historic fire report and discuss prevention today
1.y: Students read a report on the 1961 Bukit Ho Swee fire and discuss how such fires can be avoided today. One viewpoint, so partial.

2.t: Creation and progress: Students respond to news on driverless vehicles in Singapore
2.y: Students read a Singapore news item on driverless buses before class, record their thinking and discuss it. One issue, so partial at this level.

2.t: A brand-new Earth: Students read news on Singapore's climate efforts, then give their view
2.y: Students read a news item on the joint effort needed on climate change in Singapore, then type their view of the world they want to see.

1.t: Oral exam: Answering examiner questions on a video in SEC format
1.y: After viewing a video, students take part in a discussion with examiners about the video theme, giving experiences, views and reasons. Spoken, with the examiner.

1.t: Rights and duties: Students run a card-led discussion, voicing a view or its opposite
1.y: Students hold up green to share a view or red to give a contrary view in a student-run discussion on rights and duties. Discussion only, so partial.

1.t: Rights and duties: Students critique a short story or poem and write an essay
1.y: Students learn the steps of a literary critique, critique a story or poem they read, then write an essay of at least 200 words. Written, one-way.

1.t: Traditions and customs: Students agree or disagree with reasons in a student-run talk
1.y: Students sit in a circle with colour cups showing readiness, discuss objects from the opening page and agree or disagree with evidence.

1.t: Nation-building: Students analyse an interview, then role-play both sides
1.y: Students judge the purpose of a published interview and what its interviewer should and should not have done, then act out interview roles.

2.t: Entrepreneurship: Students rank skills with evidence, revise after peers, report a stance
2.y: Students rank problem solving and perseverance with evidence, discuss with peers, revise their view, and one member presents the group stance.

2.t: Entrepreneurship: Students write a CV and an official email, with teacher comments
2.y: Students build a personal CV, share it, then write an official email for a given situation and receive teacher feedback. One-way writing.

2.t: A brand-new Earth: Students share a drama critique and field classmates' questions
2.y: Students critique a drama they read, share it, and classmates comment or ask questions before teacher feedback. Written then shared.

1.t: Traditions and customs: Students explain which old objects have changed for today's world
1.y: Students pick out objects that have changed to suit present-day life and give reasons, comparing past and present uses. Comparison only.

2.t: Creation and progress: Students compare the same news in English and Tamil papers
2.y: Students compare two versions of one news story (headlines, pictures, word choice, style), then translate an English item into Tamil. Compares without linking to a change of view.

1.t: Nation-building: Students list what they know and want to know about a historic event
1.y: Before reading, students use a KWL form to share what they know and want to know about Singapore's separation from Malaysia.

2.t: A brand-new Earth: Students answer opinion questions on war and peace before reading
2.y: Before reading, students note their views on causes of war and what people must do for peace, then read and compare their answers.

1.t: Rights and duties: Students look up basic rights and duties before class
1.y: Before class, students look up information on basic rights and duties from a web page, then discuss it in a student-run discussion.

1.t: Traditions and customs: Students find out what the pictured objects were used for
1.y: Before class, students look up how the objects on the opening page were used, then compare notes in discussion.

2.t: A brand-new Earth: Students gather information on a chosen ASEAN country
2.y: Before class, each student picks one ASEAN country and collects information on it for use in the lesson.

1.t: Nation-building: Students reflect on the unit and get one-to-one feedback
1.y: Students assess their own learning in the unit, write a reflection, share it, and then get individual feedback from the teacher on how to improve.

2.t: A brand-new Earth: Students express the world they want to see in a form of their choice
2.y: Students show the world they want to see as a drawing, poem, speech or short skit, and type their view on the class board.
